The space station hung in the silent void, a solitary sentinel orbiting a planet that had long since surrendered its atmosphere to the cold vacuum of space. This desolate world, once perhaps vibrant with life or industry, now presented a face of cracked, grey crusts and deep, shadowed canyons, devoid of any sign of habitation. The station itself was a marvel of utilitarian engineering, its metallic corridors stretching into the gloom, lined with pipes and conduits that pulsed with a faint, rhythmic light. The air within was recycled and sterile, carrying the constant, low-frequency hum of life-support systems and navigation computers, a sound so pervasive it had become the heartbeat of the station’s few inhabitants.

Outside the thick, reinforced viewing ports, the universe unfolded in stark contrast to the station’s enclosed sterility. A ballet of asteroids drifted through the blackness, their jagged forms catching the distant light of a dying star. They moved in a slow, gravitational dance, tumbling and colliding in the vast emptiness, their surfaces pitted and ancient. This celestial choreography served as a haunting backdrop to the station’s isolation, a reminder of the chaotic beauty of the cosmos that lay just beyond the glass, indifferent to the fragile existence within.
